raw_answer_text:
A1: The first 32-bit word contains the Source Port and Destination Port fields, each 16 bits wide.
A2: The Sequence Number normally indicates the sequence number of the first data byte in the segment; when SYN is set, it instead represents the Initial Sequence Number (ISN), and the first actual data byte (if any) is at sequence number ISN+1.
A3: The Acknowledgment Number is valid only when the ACK control bit is set; when valid, it contains the next sequence number the sender of the segment expects to receive (i.e., one greater than the last byte successfully received).
A4: Data Offset specifies the length of the TCP header in 32-bit words; its minimum valid value is 5, corresponding to a minimum header length of 20 bytes (no options).
A5: The same word also contains a Reserved field (typically 3 or 4 bits, depending on the RFC version), the Control/Flag bits (6 or 9 bits such as URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, FIN), and the Window field (16 bits).
A6: The checksum covers the TCP header and data, plus a pseudo-header consisting of the source and destination IP addresses, the protocol number, and the TCP segment length (from the IP header), padded with zero if needed.
A7: The Urgent Pointer is meaningful only when the URG control bit is set; when applicable, it indicates the offset from the sequence number in the segment to the last byte of urgent data, marking the end of urgent data within the segment.
A8: The Options field appears only when the Data Offset value is greater than 5 (i.e., options are present, padded to a 32-bit boundary); the maximum total TCP header length, including options, is 60 bytes (Data Offset value of 15 × 4 bytes).
